idiom_name: no in-language lock: one owning task or a serializing queue per resource, Web Locks for cross-worker resources
implementation_notes: JavaScript has no intra-thread preemption: statements between two await points cannot be interrupted, and other tasks interleaving at await boundaries are not excluded by any lock object, so the classic Lock Strategy plus guard has nothing to plug into on the main thread. Shared mutable state is normally avoided (workers exchange structured-clone copies) or confined to a single owning task; when mutual exclusion across awaited steps is genuinely required it is expressed as a serializing promise chain or a userland mutex, and resources shared across workers or tabs are coordinated with the Web Locks API (navigator.locks.request, also exposed experimentally by Node) while worker-level shared memory uses Atomics over SharedArrayBuffer. If a project insists on the pattern's shape, make the strategy a higher-order function - runUnderLock(strategy, fn) - rather than an abstract Lock class.
pitfalls: A mutex held across await does not stop other tasks from running the rest of the codebase; unless every access path routes through the same strategy, the exclusion is imaginary.

Web Locks are scoped to an origin and shared with every tab of it, so a lock held across a slow or suspended task stalls all of them - keep the critical section short and never hold one while waiting for user input.
SharedArrayBuffer requires cross-origin isolation headers in browsers, and Atomics.wait is blocking and cannot be used on the main thread (use Atomics.waitAsync there).
alternative: Give each resource exactly one owning task, or funnel access through a serializing promise queue; exchange state between workers by message passing (structured clone) instead of sharing memory, and use Web Locks or Atomics only for resources genuinely shared across workers or tabs.
